facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Leverage on carrying debt rose from 3.49x of reported EBITDA at the end of 2024 to 5.37x at the end of 2025, then fell to 3.52x on a last-twelve-months basis at September 30, 2026. Net leverage followed, from 4.90x to 2.95x. For creditors the balance sheet has absorbed the 2025 shareholder-return programme, but the pending buyout can reset the debt regardless of this trajectory. limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- High: The executed credit agreement, its amendments, the full guarantor list and the restricted-group definition are not supplied, so covenant definitions, baskets, prepayment and change-of-control terms and whether the revolver's springing maturity of 2028-06-22 still applies after the 2025 amendments are not established; this restricts any statement on covenant capacity, structural priority and recovery, and it is closed only by supplying the executed documents. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 161; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 184; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18 - High: The treatment of the term loan and revolver at the closing of the pending buyout, the buyer's financing and the pro forma capital structure are not stated in the supplied documents, so no pro forma net debt or leverage is given and the post-balance-sheet table shows none; the merger agreement and financing papers would close this. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 29–30; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 51–53 - Medium: The annual scheduled-payments table places USD 1,238.858 million in 2030 although the same note and the latest quarterly report state a maturity of 2032-01-23 with quarterly payments to 2031-12-31, so the maturity ladder by year is not reliable and the chart shows the schedule as printed; the executed agreement or an issuer clarification would resolve it. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 161; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 159; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18 - Medium: No source states whether any cash is restricted or trapped, so cash and net debt are stated on cash and cash equivalents as printed and cash availability is not confirmed; an issuer statement on restrictions would close this. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 129 - Low: The issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is constructed from net income, interest, tax and depreciation and amortization, and the add-backs behind adjusted EBITDA carry no stated realisation status; the constructed figure reconciles to the issuer's adjusted figure in every column, but component support for the add-backs would be needed to normalise earnings. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 110–111; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12 - Low: No fourth-quarter 2025 report is supplied, so that quarter is derived as the full year less nine months; cash flows are reported year-to-date only, so discrete second and third quarter cash flows are derived by difference where needed; maintenance and growth capex are not split, no backlog is disclosed, and the current term loan and revolver floors and the revolver margin and spread are not printed. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 129–132; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5–8 - Low: Presentation differences remain unreconciled in the source: earnings-release headline total debt switches between principal and net carrying amount, printed lines differ by USD 1 thousand in the second-quarter cost of revenues and by up to USD 2 thousand between year-to-date and summed quarterly adjusted EBITDA, segment-note depreciation differs from cash flow depreciation by USD 131 thousand, and source dashes in the statements are written as not supplied rather than zero. Basis: EX-99.1_2026-04-30_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; EX-99.1_2026-07-30_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccc-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 178

New debt came only through the 2025 amendments: USD 225.0 million of incremental term loans on January 6, 2025 alongside the EvolutionIQ purchase, a refinancing on January 23, 2025 that extended all term loans to 2032, and USD 300.0 million of incremental term loans on December 12, 2025 that funded an accelerated share repurchase. No new term debt was issued in the first nine months of 2026, and the filings do not say how the term loan is treated at closing.

facts.text: The only acquisition the filings describe since 2022 was EvolutionIQ, completed on January 6, 2025 for $674.3 million, of which 37.14% was paid in shares. It contributed 4.0% of 2025 revenue and a pre-tax loss of $89.2 million, which included $56.7 million of stock compensation and $19.1 million of intangible amortisation, so integration has not yet added earnings. Separately, the preferred holder in the China parent company gave redemption notice on March 17, 2025, and its claim now sits as a note without recourse to the company. facts.label: Company description
facts.text: CCC runs insurance claims and collision-repair workflows on a subscription software and artificial-intelligence platform, so its cash flow is a function of how many insurers and repairers use the platform and how much each pays. One cloud platform connects hundreds of insurers, tens of thousands of repair facilities and thousands of parts suppliers and automakers, which makes each added participant more valuable to the others and leaving costly. Software subscriptions are 95.85% of nine-month 2026 revenue, insurer contracts run about three to five years and repairer contracts about three years, and no customer exceeded 10% of 2025 revenue. For creditors this gives high cash-flow visibility and a low chance of a sudden revenue break, but the franchise depends on staying embedded in United States auto claims. facts.text: Revenue is predictable and recurring rather than cyclical, with growth coming mainly from existing customers. Software subscriptions grew 10.11% in the first nine months of 2026, about 8% of the 10.55% total growth came from existing customer upgrades and expanded solutions and about 2% from new customers, and software net dollar retention rose from 105% to 108% in a year while gross retention eased from 99% to 98%. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Margins can be defended under moderate volume pressure but are flattered by lower stock compensation. Cost of revenues is 25.98% of nine-month revenue against 26.59% a year earlier because fixed-cost arrangements give scale economies, and the issuer's adjusted EBITDA margin was 42.57% for the last twelve months against 41.25% for 2025. Reported EBITDA is 31.70% of revenue, and 44.34% of its nine-month rise came from lower stock compensation, which the issuer adds back in its own measure. The mechanism is operating leverage on a largely fixed cost base, with USD 164.5 million of purchase commitments for data, hosting and software through 2031; the implication is that a revenue fall would cut margin through the same fixed base that lifted it as revenue grew. facts.label: PEST analysis
facts.text: Technology is the factor that matters for credit: artificial intelligence can extend the platform, as management's run rate of about USD 130 million, up 40%, suggests, or erode it if insurers build their own tools, so it is both the main growth driver and the main competitive risk. Regulation and litigation matter second: insurance and data regulation touch the software directly, and several putative class actions challenge the total loss valuation tool, with insurance cover and contract protection that the company says may not be adequate in every case. The economic factor is interest rates, through the floating-rate term loan. Political and social factors, including the small China business at 0.60% of revenue, do not appear to be a primary credit driver on the evidence supplied. facts.label: SWOT analysis
facts.text: Strengths are recurring subscription revenue, a retention profile with net expansion, high free cash flow conversion, a long and light maturity profile and USD 451.9 million of liquidity. Weaknesses are reliance on United States auto claims, margins flattered by lower stock compensation, a floating-rate loan with a finite hedge and limited ownership and board visibility. Opportunities that could improve credit quality are artificial-intelligence adoption, expansion into disability and workers' compensation claims, and repayment of the term loan at par in the sale. Threats that could weaken it are debt placed above or beside the term loan by the buyers, insurer in-sourcing, a failed closing with a USD 149.52 million fee, and adverse class-action outcomes. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 46; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C05; calculation C09

facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over the next 12 to 24 months the operating outlook is favourable and the capital structure outlook is open. Management's last full-year guidance, from July 30, 2026, implied revenue growth of 9.56% to 10.12% and adjusted EBITDA growth of 11.23% to 12.60%, and the third quarter beat the top of its quarterly guidance by 0.89% on revenue and 8.78% on adjusted EBITDA, which supports continued growth near 10%. Guidance was then suspended with the merger, so the forward view is no longer management's own. Tailwinds are rising retention, the artificial-intelligence run rate and cost reductions; headwinds are the swap expiry on July 31, 2027, the revolver's springing date in 2028 and the unknown buyer financing, with closing expected in the first quarter of 2027. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The most credible downside starts with insurers moving claims workflows to in-house or technology-provider tools, which the company names as competitors. The first operating break would be weaker upsell, shown in net dollar retention falling toward 100% from 108%, followed by contract losses at renewal. As an analyst assumption, not a forecast, those losses take 10% off revenue; with full flow-through to EBITDA and no cost action that would remove USD 113.92 million of earnings, lift gross leverage on the issuer's adjusted measure to 3.42x from 2.62x, and cut free cash flow to USD 197.46 million before any tax effect. If rates also rose 100 bp on the whole loan after the hedge ends, free cash flow would be USD 184.65 million and adjusted cash interest cover 4.35x. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 25; calculation C13

facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress in that scenario: free cash flow still covers scheduled amortisation 14.17x, USD 451.9 million of liquidity remains, no maturity falls due before the revolver's springing date, and management could cut capital spending, which is 5.90% of revenue, and discretionary costs. The primary downside path is therefore not operating failure but a capital structure shock: new buyer debt on top of a revenue setback, at a time when the hedge has ended, would leave less room than the operating numbers alone imply. The observable trigger is the disclosure of the buyer's financing and the treatment of the term loan. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, CCC presents a strong business profile supported by recurring subscription revenue, net retention and a network that is hard to replicate, but credit quality is constrained by the pending take-private, a floating-rate loan with a finite hedge, margins flattered by lower stock compensation and concentration in United States auto claims. Cash-flow durability appears strong because free cash flow is 27.33% of revenue and covers scheduled amortisation 23.89x. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the treatment of the term loan at closing, the buyers' financing and the revolver's 2028 springing date. The primary downside path is a capital structure shock layered on a modest revenue setback. Further analysis would require the merger agreement, the credit agreement, agency ratings and market prices. Top risk: the take-private resets the capital structure ahead of existing lenders. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation C05; calculation C09

## Findings
### Bottom line

The seven supplied filings support the requested financial, transaction and credit-synthesis work on CCC, but the missing credit agreement and merger agreement leave the treatment of the term loan in the pending buyout unresolved for creditors. The debt in the filings is one senior secured term loan of USD 1,281.2 million principal and an undrawn USD 250.0 million revolver at September 30, 2026, and the statements, debt note and non-GAAP reconciliations cover FY2025 and each 2026 quarter through Q3.

The buyout at USD 7.75 per share in cash, agreed on October 14, 2026 and expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, is described only in summary: the filings give conditions and termination fees but do not say how the existing debt is treated at closing. The latest supplied document is dated October 29, 2026, seven days before the as-of date, and peer, market, rating, portfolio and executed-legal-document inputs are absent, so the modules that need them cannot run.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage on carrying debt fell from 5.37x of reported EBITDA at year-end 2025 to 3.52x at September 30, 2026 on a last-twelve-months basis, but the pending buyout leaves the term loan's treatment open for creditors. Net debt over reported EBITDA fell from 4.90x to 2.95x, and the issuer's adjusted measure gives 2.62x gross.
Basis: calculation C09; calculation C10; calculation C14

Part of the improvement is lower stock compensation, a non-cash charge that depresses reported EBITDA, so cash generation is the firmer test: cash interest cover was 4.98x on the same basis. The debt is one floating-rate term loan maturing in 2032 and an undrawn revolver maturing in 2029, subject to a springing 2028 maturity that the filings state but do not settle.
Basis: calculation C11; calculation C17; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18

### Financial interpretation

Leverage on carrying debt rose from 3.49x of reported EBITDA at the end of 2024 to 5.37x at the end of 2025, then fell to 3.52x on a last-twelve-months basis at September 30, 2026. The 2025 rise came from USD 525.0 million of new term loans, which funded the EvolutionIQ acquisition and share repurchases, while cash fell from USD 398.983 million to USD 111.192 million; the 2026 fall comes from higher earnings, scheduled amortisation and a rebuilt cash balance, with no further term-loan issuance. Net leverage followed, from 4.90x to 2.95x. For creditors the balance sheet has absorbed the 2025 shareholder-return programme, but the pending buyout can reset the debt regardless of this trajectory.

Basis: calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C09; calculation C10; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 158–161; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 132; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 8

Reported EBITDA is the primary denominator here and is depressed by non-cash stock compensation, which the issuer adds back to reach adjusted EBITDA; on the issuer's measure leverage is 2.62x gross and 2.20x net at September 30, 2026. About 44% of the nine-month rise in reported EBITDA comes from lower stock compensation rather than higher adjusted earnings, so the reported deleveraging overstates operating progress and the adjusted view is the cleaner read of cash earnings. The add-backs are management-defined and are not classified as realised or unrealised in the sources, so creditors should treat the adjusted ratios as a supporting view only.
Basis: calculation C06; calculation C13; calculation C14; calculation C17; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 110–111; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12

Cash interest cover on reported EBITDA improved from 3.57x for 2025 to 4.98x for the twelve months to September 30, 2026, because cash interest paid rose only modestly while earnings grew. The term loan is floating-rate and the swaps that fix USD 750.0 million of it at about 3.94% run only to July 31, 2027, so the cover benefits from a hedge that is finite; the sensitivity after that date is not established here and belongs to Rates, FX & hedging.
Basis: calculation C07; calculation C11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 18–19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 46

Cash generation is solid after capital spending: free cash flow was USD 254.508 million for 2025 and USD 311.375 million for the twelve months to September 30, 2026. Working capital was a drag in 2026: deferred revenues, which are customer advances that fund operations without interest, fell from USD 72.793 million at year-end to USD 54.917 million, a decrease the quarterly report attributes to the timing of revenue recognition. If billing terms shortened, that float would absorb cash ahead of any earnings decline, so Earnings quality and Liquidity should watch it.
Basis: calculation C16; calculation C18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 47

Liquidity is adequate on filed figures: cash of USD 202.926 million plus USD 249.0 million of undrawn revolver availability, against about USD 13.033 million a year of scheduled amortisation and cash interest of USD 72.448 million over the last twelve months, with no stated maturity before the revolver's 2029 date, subject to the springing test noted below. The weak points are the unconfirmed availability of cash, because no source states whether any cash is restricted, the revolver's springing maturity on 2028-06-22, whose application after the 2025 amendments cannot be settled without the executed agreement, and the merger agreement's limits on new debt, dividends and certain capital spending, which constrain management's response to a shock.
Basis: calculation C07; calculation C15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 46; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 52

The pending merger is a subsequent event and is not blended into any figure. It states no financing condition, but the filings do not say whether the term loan stays in place, is repaid or carries change-of-control terms, so the pro forma capital structure is not established; a termination fee of USD 149.52 million payable by the company in some circumstances would be a claim on liquidity if the agreement fails.

Debt appears on two bases in the filings, carrying value of USD 1,269.596 million and principal of USD 1,281.216 million at September 30, 2026, and the earnings releases switch between them from quarter to quarter. Carrying value is the right basis for leverage, and principal is the amount a refinancing or the buyout would have to address, a difference of USD 11.620 million; the minority-investor note of USD 27.562 million is without recourse to the company and is kept outside debt.
Basis: calculation C01; calculation C19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5

The most material data-quality risks are the annual maturity schedule that places the whole balance in 2030 against a stated 2032 maturity, the absence of any restricted-cash statement, and the construction of reported EBITDA, which the issuer does not state. Each is logged under the gaps; none changes the carrying-debt figures, which tie between the balance sheet, the debt note and the cash flow statement.
Basis: calculation C12; calculation C19; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 161; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19

- High: The executed credit agreement, its amendments, the full guarantor list and the restricted-group definition are not supplied, so covenant definitions, baskets, prepayment and change-of-control terms and whether the revolver's springing maturity of 2028-06-22 still applies after the 2025 amendments are not established; this restricts any statement on covenant capacity, structural priority and recovery, and it is closed only by supplying the executed documents.

- High: The treatment of the term loan and revolver at the closing of the pending buyout, the buyer's financing and the pro forma capital structure are not stated in the supplied documents, so no pro forma net debt or leverage is given and the post-balance-sheet table shows none; the merger agreement and financing papers would close this.

- Medium: The annual scheduled-payments table places USD 1,238.858 million in 2030 although the same note and the latest quarterly report state a maturity of 2032-01-23 with quarterly payments to 2031-12-31, so the maturity ladder by year is not reliable and the chart shows the schedule as printed; the executed agreement or an issuer clarification would resolve it.

- Medium: No source states whether any cash is restricted or trapped, so cash and net debt are stated on cash and cash equivalents as printed and cash availability is not confirmed; an issuer statement on restrictions would close this.

- Low: The issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is constructed from net income, interest, tax and depreciation and amortization, and the add-backs behind adjusted EBITDA carry no stated realisation status; the constructed figure reconciles to the issuer's adjusted figure in every column, but component support for the add-backs would be needed to normalise earnings.

- Low: No fourth-quarter 2025 report is supplied, so that quarter is derived as the full year less nine months; cash flows are reported year-to-date only, so discrete second and third quarter cash flows are derived by difference where needed; maintenance and growth capex are not split, no backlog is disclosed, and the current term loan and revolver floors and the revolver margin and spread are not printed.

- Low: Presentation differences remain unreconciled in the source: earnings-release headline total debt switches between principal and net carrying amount, printed lines differ by USD 1 thousand in the second-quarter cost of revenues and by up to USD 2 thousand between year-to-date and summed quarterly adjusted EBITDA, segment-note depreciation differs from cash flow depreciation by USD 131 thousand, and source dashes in the statements are written as not supplied rather than zero.

## Findings
### Bottom line

CCC is a recurring-revenue software platform with a broad customer base, but its pending sale to a consortium led by GTCR leaves the senior secured term loan's treatment unstated, which is the one fact that could change creditor protection. Software subscriptions are 95.85% of nine-month 2026 revenue, no customer exceeded 10% of 2025 revenue, and contracted revenue due within a year equals 70.75% of last-twelve-months revenue, so the operating base supports debt service.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 29–30; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C02; calculation C09; calculation C13

Governance gives creditors limited visibility. The filings name no controlling holder, the finance and technology chiefs are interim, and the proxy statement that would carry ownership and board detail is not supplied. The documented pattern is shareholder-favouring and partly debt-funded: in 2025 the company borrowed USD 525.0 million of new term loans and repurchased USD 600.57 million of its shares.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 158–159; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 132; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccc-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 47; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 54; Source readiness (CP-0); calculation C14
### Key findings

The operating model supports debt service because revenue is overwhelmingly subscription-based and spread across a broad customer base. Software subscriptions grew 10.11% in the first nine months of 2026, about 8% of the 10.55% revenue growth came from existing customers and about 2% from new ones, no customer exceeded 10% of revenue in any of the last three years, and software net dollar retention was 108% in the third quarter against gross retention of 98%, so existing customers expand more than they leave. Contracted revenue of USD 1,808 million is 1.59x last-twelve-months revenue, but it is USD 83 million lower than at year-end.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 39; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 149; calculation C10; calculation C13

Margin gains are real but partly non-cash, so cash earnings improved by less than the margin suggests. Operating income rose to 17.86% of revenue from 5.61% in the first nine months of 2026, but 47.62% of the rise in operating income came from lower stock compensation, a non-cash cost, with the rest from revenue growth outpacing cost growth.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 39; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; calculation C06; calculation C20

Customer concentration is low but end-market concentration is high, so the main business risk is a shift in United States auto-claims activity or in how insurers buy technology, not the loss of one customer. Nearly all revenue is earned in the United States, at 99.40% of nine-month 2026 revenue; the company names insurers' in-house systems and large horizontal technology providers as competitors; and part of revenue depends on claim volumes rather than subscriptions. The filings do not split revenue by insurer, repairer or other solution, so exposure by customer group is not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation C11

The pending take-private is the dominant creditor event, and the filings do not say what happens to the existing debt. The buyers agreed to pay $7.75 per share, an enterprise value of about $6.1bn that is 12.58x last-twelve-months issuer-adjusted EBITDA and puts the term loan principal at 21.00% of that value. That cushion is large at the offer price, but new buyer debt would use it, and the filings refer to the buyer's equity, debt or preferred equity financing without stating amounts, ranking or which entity borrows.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 29–30; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C05

Control cannot be assessed beyond what the filings state, which weakens any view on who can consent to amendments or liability management. No beneficial-ownership table is supplied, an unnamed principal equity owner appears only through secondary-offering and related-party disclosures, and its stake is not given. Selling stockholders sold shares equal to 59.33% of today's share count in secondary offerings from 2023 to 2025, which shows a large sell-down but not who now controls the vote.

Documented capital allocation favours shareholders and has been partly debt-funded, which is creditor-adverse in direction but has not involved liability management. In December 2025 the company raised $300.0 million of incremental term loans to fund an accelerated share repurchase, and it bought shares from its principal equity owner in November 2023 and March 2025 for $400.80 million in total, at an average of $10.15 per share against the $7.75 offer. The company attributes most of a $8.7 million rise in nine-month 2026 interest expense to that loan. The filings describe no dividend, priming, drop-down or exchange transaction, and the new loans carry the same security and guarantees as the existing loan, so the behaviour raised leverage without changing lender priority.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 158–160; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 166–168; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 176; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40; calculation C15; calculation C08

The merger agreement freezes shareholder leakage until closing but adds a liquidity claim if the company walks away. Without the buyer's consent the company may not incur certain debt, pay dividends, repurchase shares or make certain capital expenditures, and a termination fee of $149.52 million, equal to 73.68% of September 30 cash, is payable by the company in some circumstances, while the buyer owes about $313.99 million if it fails to fund.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 52; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 4; calculation C07

Reporting is adequate for monitoring, but management continuity and control disclosure are weak points. The audit opinion and the internal-control conclusion are clean, yet the finance chief role has been interim since the second-quarter report, the technology chief role was already described as interim at the annual report and an interim appointment was announced on July 14, 2026, one person is both chairman and chief executive, and the proxy statement is not supplied, so board independence, committee oversight and related-party policy are not established.
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case against a cautious governance view is that the buyers are paying a price that leaves a thin debt load relative to value: the term loan is 21.00% of enterprise value, the offer is 28.39% above the March 2026 repurchase price, and the credit agreement, which is not supplied, may require repayment on a change of control, which would take lenders out at par. Related-party dealings are small at 0.52% of 2025 revenue, the company states no plans to pay dividends, and revolver borrowings stayed below the 35% usage level that triggers the financial covenant at each 2026 quarter-end.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 175; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 91; 10-Q_2026-03-31_ccc-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ccc-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; calculation C05; calculation C08; calculation C16

The strongest case against the business view is that contracted revenue fell USD 83 million in nine months while revenue grew, that insurers' own systems and artificial-intelligence-led competitors are named threats, and that guidance and the earnings call were withdrawn just as the sale was announced, removing management's forward view. If the merger agreement or the credit agreement shows the term loan repaid at par, or kept with unchanged covenants and no new priority debt, governance risk would fall. Buyer debt placed at the borrower, a consent or amendment that loosens restrictions, or a failed closing that triggers the $149.52 million fee would raise it, and the 2026 proxy statement naming the principal equity owner would show who controls the vote.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 25; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation C07; calculation C13
### Limitations

- The merger agreement and the buyer's financing papers are not supplied, so the finding that the buyout can change creditor protection stays open until they show whether the term loan is repaid, assumed or amended at closing.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 53

- No source names the principal equity owner or gives ownership percentages, so the finding on who controls approvals and amendments rests on indirect evidence and could move in either direction once the 2026 proxy statement is read.

- The credit agreement's own terms on change of control, guarantors and restricted payments are not supplied, so the sponsor-behaviour finding rests on what the filings report about amendments, not on what the documents permit.
- Management changes are visible only in signature blocks and one appointment notice, with no reasons stated, so the continuity finding records the facts without a view on cause.
- Retention, customer and geography measures are management-defined and exclude small customers, casualty and ecosystem lines, so the resilience finding covers the core automotive software base only.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The company agreed on October 14, 2026 to a cash merger with Mozart Parent, LLC, under which a merger subsidiary merges into the company and the company survives as a wholly owned subsidiary of the buyer. Shareholders receive $7.75 per share. The third-quarter earnings release describes the buyers as a consortium of private investment firms led by GTCR and including Elliott Investment Management, and puts the enterprise value at about $6.1bn, while the quarterly report names only the Mozart entities. Closing is expected in the first quarter of 2027, subject to adoption by holders of a majority of the shares, expiry of the antitrust waiting period and the absence of a blocking order; the agreement has no financing condition and either side may terminate if the merger is not completed by April 14, 2027.

The buyer's funding is described only in outline: the filings say the buyer has represented that its financing will be sufficient and refer to equity financing and to debt or preferred equity financing, without amounts, lenders, ranking or the borrowing entity. Termination fees run both ways, $149.52 million payable by the company in some circumstances, including a superior proposal, and about $313.99 million payable by the buyer if it fails to fund. Until closing the company has agreed not to incur certain debt, pay dividends or repurchase its shares without the buyer's consent.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 52; calculation C07

Existing debt is one senior secured term loan, borrowed by CCC Intelligent Solutions Inc., with USD 1,281.2 million of principal at September 30, 2026 maturing on January 23, 2032, and an undrawn USD 250.0 million revolver maturing on September 23, 2029 with a springing maturity of June 22, 2028. New debt came only through the 2025 amendments: USD 225.0 million of incremental term loans on January 6, 2025 alongside the EvolutionIQ purchase, a refinancing on January 23, 2025 that extended all term loans to 2032, and USD 300.0 million of incremental term loans on December 12, 2025 that funded an accelerated share repurchase. No new term debt was issued in the first nine months of 2026, and the filings do not say how the term loan is treated at closing.

The only acquisition the filings describe since 2022 was EvolutionIQ, completed on January 6, 2025 for $674.3 million, of which 37.14% was paid in shares. It contributed 4.0% of 2025 revenue and a pre-tax loss of $89.2 million, which included $56.7 million of stock compensation and $19.1 million of intangible amortisation, so integration has not yet added earnings. Separately, the preferred holder in the China parent company gave redemption notice on March 17, 2025, and its claim now sits as a note without recourse to the company.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Fundamental credit quality is solid and improving, but the pending take-private, not operating performance, is now the main driver of creditor outcomes because it can reset leverage and the term loan's terms. Net debt is 2.95x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA, down from 4.90x at year-end 2025, free cash flow is 27.33% of revenue, and liquidity of USD 451.9 million covers cash interest 6.24x.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 45–46; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C05

The strongest support is a subscription base with software net dollar retention of 108%. The weakest points are a floating-rate loan whose USD 750.0 million hedge ends in July 2027, margin gains that are partly lower stock compensation, and a buyer whose debt plans are not stated.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation C07; calculation C11
### Key findings

The business profile is the main credit support because revenue is recurring, retained and spread across a very large customer base. Software subscriptions are 95.85% of nine-month 2026 revenue, software net dollar retention is 108% against gross retention of 98%, and contracted revenue of USD 1,808 million is 1.59x last-twelve-months revenue. No customer exceeded 10% of 2025 revenue, so the loss of one account cannot by itself break cash flow.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; calculation C10

Deleveraging is real and cash-backed, so the existing term loan is serviceable from its own cash flow. Net debt fell from 4.90x reported EBITDA at year-end 2025 to 2.95x on a last-twelve-months basis and from 2.68x to 2.20x on the issuer's adjusted measure, while free cash flow reached 27.33% of revenue and 64.21% of adjusted EBITDA and covers scheduled amortisation 23.89x. The reduction comes mostly from earnings growth and a rebuilt cash balance, not repayment: only scheduled principal was paid in 2026.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C04; calculation C05

Liquidity and maturities leave no near-term refinancing need. Cash of USD 202.9 million and USD 249.0 million of undrawn revolver give USD 451.9 million, which covers cash interest 6.24x and cash interest plus scheduled amortisation 5.29x, and the term loan matures in 5.22 years. The one date to watch is the revolver's springing maturity, 1.63 years away, which the quarterly report still recites if more than USD 234.0 million of term loan remains; the loan now matures in 2032, so the recital may be legacy wording, and only the credit agreement can settle it.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C05; calculation C06

Interest-rate exposure is the most mechanical weakness. The term loan is floating-rate, the swaps that fix USD 750.0 million at about 3.94% end on July 31, 2027, and each 100 bp on the whole loan costs USD 12.81 million a year, close to the USD 12.9 million the company stated at year-end and 4.11% of last-twelve-months free cash flow. That is manageable on today's cash flow, but the current cash interest cover of 4.98x on reported EBITDA rests on a hedge that is finite.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 46; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 124–125; calculation C03; calculation C07

Earnings quality is weaker than the headline margin suggests. The issuer's adjusted EBITDA margin is 42.57% but reported EBITDA is 31.70% of revenue, and 44.34% of the nine-month rise in reported EBITDA came from lower stock compensation, a non-cash cost, so cash earnings improved by less than the margin. Leverage on the issuer's adjusted measure is therefore a supporting view, not the primary one.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 39; calculation C02; calculation C11

The pending take-private is the swing factor for creditors. At $7.75 per share and an enterprise value of about $6.1bn, the term loan principal is 21.00% of value, which is a large cushion, but the filings do not say whether the loan is repaid, assumed or amended or what debt the buyers add. Until the merger and credit agreements are read, leverage, security and covenant conclusions apply only to the capital structure as it stands.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 29–30; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C09

Financial policy has been shareholder-favouring and partly debt-funded, which is why the buyers' plan matters. In 2025 the company borrowed USD 525.0 million of new term loans and repurchased USD 600.57 million of shares, including a $300.0 million accelerated repurchase funded by incremental term loans, and it states no plans for dividends. The behaviour raised leverage without changing lender priority, so it is a signal about tolerance, not a breach of creditor protection.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 158–159; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 168; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 91; calculation C14

The main business downside is end-market concentration, not customer concentration. 99.40% of nine-month revenue is earned in the United States, part of revenue depends on claim volumes, the company names insurers' in-house systems and large technology providers as competitors, and several putative class actions challenge the total loss valuation tool. Management's artificial-intelligence run rate of about USD 130 million, up 40%, is a growth opportunity and a competitive risk at once.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 34; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 75; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C10
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case against the solid view is that leverage on reported EBITDA is still 3.52x, was 5.37x at year-end 2025, and could rise again if the buyers finance the purchase with debt at or above the borrower, while contracted revenue fell USD 83 million in nine months and the issuer's adjusted ratios depend on add-backs that the filings do not classify. The finance chief role is interim and the last guidance has been withdrawn, so the forward view rests on analysis, not on management's own numbers.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C01; calculation C10

The strongest case for a better view is that the term loan is only 21.00% of enterprise value and the credit agreement may require repayment on a change of control, which would take lenders out at par; the third quarter also beat the top of its revenue guidance by 0.89% and of its adjusted EBITDA guidance by 8.78%. The view would improve if the merger agreement or credit agreement shows repayment at par or an unchanged loan with no priority debt added, and it would weaken if buyer debt is placed at the borrower, if the swaps are not replaced before July 2027, or if the revolver is not extended before its 2028 springing date.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); EX-99.1_2026-07-30_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; calculation C09; calculation C12

### Strengths and weaknesses

Three strengths carry the credit. Recurring, retained revenue is the first: software subscriptions are 95.85% of nine-month revenue and retention of 108% net and 98% gross means existing customers expand more than they leave, so cash flow is visible and debt service does not depend on winning new accounts. Cash conversion is the second: free cash flow after interest and capital spending is 27.33% of revenue and covers scheduled amortisation 23.89x, so the loan can be serviced and slowly repaid from operations. The third is a long, light maturity profile: the term loan matures in 5.22 years with about USD 13 million a year of amortisation and USD 451.9 million of liquidity.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; calculation C02; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C10

Four weaknesses constrain it. The take-private is the first, because debt treatment and buyer financing are unstated and the equity cushion could be used by new debt. Floating-rate exposure is the second, because the hedge on USD 750.0 million ends on July 31, 2027 and each 100 bp then costs USD 12.81 million a year. Earnings quality is the third, because lower stock compensation explains 44.34% of the rise in reported EBITDA. The fourth is concentration of the business in United States auto claims, where insurer in-house systems and artificial-intelligence-led competitors are the named threats and governance visibility is limited by an interim finance chief and an unnamed principal equity owner.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 46; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 25; calculation C07; calculation C09; calculation C11

### Company description

CCC runs insurance claims and collision-repair workflows on a subscription software and artificial-intelligence platform, so its cash flow is a function of how many insurers and repairers use the platform and how much each pays. One cloud platform connects hundreds of insurers, tens of thousands of repair facilities and thousands of parts suppliers and automakers, which makes each added participant more valuable to the others and leaving costly. Software subscriptions are 95.85% of nine-month 2026 revenue, insurer contracts run about three to five years and repairer contracts about three years, and no customer exceeded 10% of 2025 revenue. For creditors this gives high cash-flow visibility and a low chance of a sudden revenue break, but the franchise depends on staying embedded in United States auto claims.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 5–7; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; calculation C10

The 2025 purchase of EvolutionIQ extends the platform into disability and workers' compensation claims. It contributed 4.0% of 2025 revenue and lost $89.2 million before tax in that year, so it adds growth optionality but not yet earnings, and it was part-funded with USD 225.0 million of incremental term loans.

### Ownership and group structure

The company is a listed Delaware holding company that borrows through its operating subsidiary, CCC Intelligent Solutions Inc., with first-priority liens on that subsidiary's equity and substantially all its assets and guarantees from an intermediate holding company and certain United States subsidiaries. The China holding company owes a note to a minority investor, without recourse to the company, so claims on China assets sit behind that note, a small matter in a unit that earns 0.60% of revenue. No controlling holder is named and no beneficial-ownership table is supplied, an unnamed principal equity owner sold shares to the company in 2023 and 2025, and the pending sale would make the company a wholly owned subsidiary of the buyer. Control, exit intent and consent rights are therefore not established, which limits any view on who can amend the loan terms.

### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is predictable and recurring rather than cyclical, with growth coming mainly from existing customers. Software subscriptions grew 10.11% in the first nine months of 2026, about 8% of the 10.55% total growth came from existing customer upgrades and expanded solutions and about 2% from new customers, and software net dollar retention rose from 105% to 108% in a year while gross retention eased from 99% to 98%. The mechanism is switching cost and network effect: customers that depend on the platform for estimates and repair programmes pay more as they add solutions and rarely leave. The implication is revenue visibility that supports debt service, with two caveats: growth leans on upgrades and added solutions sold to existing insurer and repairer customers, and part of revenue is tied to claim volumes, which the company does not quantify.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 39; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 34; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C10

Contracted revenue of USD 1,808 million is 1.59x last-twelve-months revenue and USD 806 million falls in the next twelve months, equal to 70.75% of last-twelve-months revenue. It is USD 83 million lower than at year-end, which the filings do not explain, so it is treated as an open question and not as evidence of churn. Financial foundation lists no backlog measure, while the quarterly report states contracted revenue as remaining performance obligations; this analysis uses that figure and notes the difference.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Margins can be defended under moderate volume pressure but are flattered by lower stock compensation. Cost of revenues is 25.98% of nine-month revenue against 26.59% a year earlier because fixed-cost arrangements give scale economies, and the issuer's adjusted EBITDA margin was 42.57% for the last twelve months against 41.25% for 2025. Reported EBITDA is 31.70% of revenue, and 44.34% of its nine-month rise came from lower stock compensation, which the issuer adds back in its own measure. The mechanism is operating leverage on a largely fixed cost base, with USD 164.5 million of purchase commitments for data, hosting and software through 2031; the implication is that a revenue fall would cut margin through the same fixed base that lifted it as revenue grew.

### Capital intensity and cash conversion

Capital spending is modest and cash conversion is high, so EBITDA translates into durable free cash flow. Purchases of software, equipment and property, including capitalised development time, were 5.90% of last-twelve-months revenue, free cash flow was 27.33% of revenue and 64.21% of adjusted EBITDA, and nine-month free cash flow grew 38.00% as operating cash flow grew 32.17%. Nine-month operating cash flow absorbed a USD 23.1 million working-capital outflow, mostly lower deferred revenue, so the float that customers advance is shrinking; if billing terms shortened it would absorb cash ahead of any earnings fall. Cash interest is the main fixed charge and is covered 4.98x by reported EBITDA and 6.69x by adjusted EBITDA.

### Porter's five forces

Competitive rivalry is moderate and mostly indirect. The company's competitors are customers' own software, insurance software vendors, large horizontal technology providers and niche vendors, and the market is described as fragmented, so rivalry shows up as pricing pressure at renewal rather than as lost share today; retention of 108% net and 98% gross says it is not yet costing revenue.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 25–26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; calculation C10

The threat of new entrants is limited by the network, which took decades to build, by integrations with hundreds of insurers and tens of thousands of repairers, and by years of claims data, so a new entrant needs both sides of the market at once. Large technology providers with artificial-intelligence capability and insurer relationships are the exception, and they could attack one workflow at a time, which would pressure pricing before it moved revenue.

Substitutes are the main force: insurers can build or buy claims software, and artificial-intelligence tools could automate steps that the platform now charges for. The company itself lists changes in customers' perceptions of artificial intelligence as a risk. Buyer power sits with large insurers, since the company serves 27 of the top 30 auto carriers, and some arrangements can be cancelled or not renewed on relatively short notice, although no customer exceeded 10% of 2025 revenue. Supplier power comes from licensed data and cloud hosting, with fixed purchase commitments of USD 164.5 million, which raises the cost base but does not threaten service continuity on the evidence supplied.
### PEST analysis

Technology is the factor that matters for credit: artificial intelligence can extend the platform, as management's run rate of about USD 130 million, up 40%, suggests, or erode it if insurers build their own tools, so it is both the main growth driver and the main competitive risk. Regulation and litigation matter second: insurance and data regulation touch the software directly, and several putative class actions challenge the total loss valuation tool, with insurance cover and contract protection that the company says may not be adequate in every case. The economic factor is interest rates, through the floating-rate term loan. Political and social factors, including the small China business at 0.60% of revenue, do not appear to be a primary credit driver on the evidence supplied.

### SWOT analysis

Strengths are recurring subscription revenue, a retention profile with net expansion, high free cash flow conversion, a long and light maturity profile and USD 451.9 million of liquidity. Weaknesses are reliance on United States auto claims, margins flattered by lower stock compensation, a floating-rate loan with a finite hedge and limited ownership and board visibility. Opportunities that could improve credit quality are artificial-intelligence adoption, expansion into disability and workers' compensation claims, and repayment of the term loan at par in the sale. Threats that could weaken it are debt placed above or beside the term loan by the buyers, insurer in-sourcing, a failed closing with a USD 149.52 million fee, and adverse class-action outcomes.

The business assessments are strong where the evidence is specific and average where it is not. Scale and market position are strong because the platform serves 27 of the top 30 auto carriers and all of the national multi-shop repair operators, competitive advantage is strong because network integration and retention of 108% net and 98% gross are hard to replicate, and diversification is average because customers are spread across many accounts but revenue sits almost entirely in United States auto claims.

The earnings assessments are average to strong. Cost and capex flexibility is average because costs are largely fixed but capital spending is only 5.90% of revenue, margin stability is average because the margin gain is partly lower stock compensation, and free cash flow stability is strong because conversion is 64.21% of adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow covers scheduled amortisation 23.89x.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C02; calculation C04; calculation C05; calculation C15

The capital assessments are strong for liquidity and average for market access and policy. Liquidity is strong at USD 451.9 million against a 6.24x cash interest need; ability to refinance is average because the maturities are long but the springing revolver date and the buyer's financing are unsettled and no rating or market price is supplied; financial policy and governance are average because debt-funded repurchases coexist with transparent reporting, covenant compliance and small related-party flows. The trend is improving on leverage and cash flow, and the key missing datapoints are the merger and credit agreements and the 2026 proxy statement.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C14
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the operating outlook is favourable and the capital structure outlook is open. Management's last full-year guidance, from July 30, 2026, implied revenue growth of 9.56% to 10.12% and adjusted EBITDA growth of 11.23% to 12.60%, and the third quarter beat the top of its quarterly guidance by 0.89% on revenue and 8.78% on adjusted EBITDA, which supports continued growth near 10%. Guidance was then suspended with the merger, so the forward view is no longer management's own. Tailwinds are rising retention, the artificial-intelligence run rate and cost reductions; headwinds are the swap expiry on July 31, 2027, the revolver's springing date in 2028 and the unknown buyer financing, with closing expected in the first quarter of 2027.

Basis: EX-99.1_2026-07-30_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; EX-99.1_2026-10-29_ccc-ex99_1.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 29–30; calculation C06; calculation C12; calculation C16

Over three to five years the question is whether artificial intelligence widens the moat or opens it. Adoption by insurers of the company's own artificial-intelligence tools could support pricing and retention, while in-house and technology-provider alternatives would pressure renewals, and the term loan itself matures in 2032 with only scheduled amortisation in between. For creditors, the medium-term risk to the debt comes from capital structure choices by the buyers more than from the operating outlook.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; calculation C06
### Downside scenario

The most credible downside starts with insurers moving claims workflows to in-house or technology-provider tools, which the company names as competitors. The first operating break would be weaker upsell, shown in net dollar retention falling toward 100% from 108%, followed by contract losses at renewal. As an analyst assumption, not a forecast, those losses take 10% off revenue; with full flow-through to EBITDA and no cost action that would remove USD 113.92 million of earnings, lift gross leverage on the issuer's adjusted measure to 3.42x from 2.62x, and cut free cash flow to USD 197.46 million before any tax effect. If rates also rose 100 bp on the whole loan after the hedge ends, free cash flow would be USD 184.65 million and adjusted cash interest cover 4.35x.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-K_2025-12-31_ccc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 25; calculation C13

Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress in that scenario: free cash flow still covers scheduled amortisation 14.17x, USD 451.9 million of liquidity remains, no maturity falls due before the revolver's springing date, and management could cut capital spending, which is 5.90% of revenue, and discretionary costs. The primary downside path is therefore not operating failure but a capital structure shock: new buyer debt on top of a revenue setback, at a time when the hedge has ended, would leave less room than the operating numbers alone imply. The observable trigger is the disclosure of the buyer's financing and the treatment of the term loan.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation C05; calculation C13; calculation C15
### Overall credit view

Overall, CCC presents a strong business profile supported by recurring subscription revenue, net retention and a network that is hard to replicate, but credit quality is constrained by the pending take-private, a floating-rate loan with a finite hedge, margins flattered by lower stock compensation and concentration in United States auto claims. Cash-flow durability appears strong because free cash flow is 27.33% of revenue and covers scheduled amortisation 23.89x. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the treatment of the term loan at closing, the buyers' financing and the revolver's 2028 springing date. The primary downside path is a capital structure shock layered on a modest revenue setback. Further analysis would require the merger agreement, the credit agreement, agency ratings and market prices. Top risk: the take-private resets the capital structure ahead of existing lenders.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ccc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 51; calculation C05; calculation C09
